## Contents and purpose

This script's job is to calculate standard deviation of entropy values PER SAMPLE, once for each method (plugin, Chao-Shen, CWJ and SpaNorm).
To do so it will take the resulting .csv tables that come from the previous script's results (so from those of `01_load_and_compute_entropy/tables/`, `03_compute_alternative_entropies/tables/` and `06_compute_spanorm_entropy/tables/`) and will make a new script that has a separate ranking for each method, in order to find out what are the samples with the highest variability.

### 1. Dependencies and configuration

No particular packages are required since this is just some regular R stuff and .csv manipulation.
We will still use `here` to be consistent with the previous script's way of handling file paths.

```{R}
#| eval: false
library(here)
```

We can easily recycle the same input and output handling structure we've been using since script 01, by creating paths from the previous script's results and creating a new results folder for this script, which will just contain a `tables/` subfolder.

Let's select our inputs like we're used to:

```{R}
dir_input_plugin  <- here::here("results", "01_load_and_compute_entropy", "tables")
dir_input_alt     <- here::here("results", "03_compute_alternative_entropies", "tables")
dir_input_spanorm <- here::here("results", "06_compute_spanorm_entropy", "tables")
```

Then we take care of our outputs:

```{R}
dir_results <- here::here("results", "09_entropy_standard_deviation")
dir_tables  <- file.path(dir_results, "tables")
```

We could make it simpler by directly creating the `tables/` subfolder in one go but let's keep this consistent with our previous work.
Again we add the directory creation line but it will not be needed after GitHub cloning:

```{R}
dir.create(dir_tables, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

Now since we have to handle many different lists (at most 22 x 4 if we decide to run the script on all samples), we'll naturally initialize a list of files coming from our previously selected input directories like this:

```{R}
all_csv_files <- list.files(dir_input_plugin, pattern = "_entropy\\.csv$", full.names = FALSE)
```

I don't know why I'm so dumb with regex but I used AI again to make the most compact regex selection for our use case.

We can now do our usual trick for having ordered sample processing:

```{R}
all_samples   <- gsub("_entropy\\.csv$", "", all_csv_files)
sample_numbers <- as.numeric(gsub("sample", "", all_samples))
all_samples    <- all_samples[order(sample_numbers)]
```

Now the good old sample selection toggle, and the if else that handles what the `samples_to_process` variable will be:

```{R}
if (identical(SAMPLES_TO_RUN, "all")) {
  samples_to_process <- all_samples
} else {
  samples_to_process <- SAMPLES_TO_RUN
}
```

We're good to go on with the scripts actual logic.


### 2. Processing loop

Let's start by initializing an empty list, where we'll store our dataframes as they get generated.

```{R}
summary_list <- list()
```

Then, once again, we start a loop that will repeat the logic for each sample we selected.

```{R}
for (sample in samples_to_process) {
  
  message("\nProcessing: ", sample_name)
```

#### A. Load tables

We set where the .csv tables would come from previously, now we actually define their file based on the sample we're currently processing:

```{R}
  file_plugin  <- file.path(dir_input_plugin,  paste0(sample_name, "_entropy.csv"))
  file_alt     <- file.path(dir_input_alt,     paste0(sample_name, "_alternative_entropies.csv"))
  file_spanorm <- file.path(dir_input_spanorm, paste0(sample_name, "_spanorm_entropy.csv"))
```

Since our script depends on the output of previous files, it's reasonable to set a check for the existance of such output, so that the user is informed that he still has something to run:

```{R}
  if (!file.exists(file_plugin) || !file.exists(file_alt) || !file.exists(file_spanorm)) {
    warning("Missing input files for ", sample_name, ". Skipping...")
    next
  }
```


We can finally load our beloved .csvs into R:

```{R}
  df_plugin  <- read.csv(file_plugin,  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  df_alt     <- read.csv(file_alt,     stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  df_spanorm <- read.csv(file_spanorm, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

#### B. Compute standard deviation

Let's now get to the actual calculation of the standard deviation.
It is actually pretty intuitive as we just need to use the `sd()` R function on the appropriate columns of our tables.

```{R}
  sd_plugin    <- sd(df_plugin$entropy[is.finite(df_plugin$entropy)])
  sd_chao_shen <- sd(df_alt$chao_shen_entropy[is.finite(df_alt$chao_shen_entropy)])
  sd_cwj       <- sd(df_alt$cwj_entropy[is.finite(df_alt$cwj_entropy)])
  sd_spanorm   <- sd(df_spanorm$spanorm_entropy[is.finite(df_spanorm[[spanorm_col]])])
```

The `is.finite()` is needed to exclude NA spots if they are present (possible if there are spots with 0 counts in tissue in the RDS object that generated them, for which the entropy is not defined).

Now that we have the values we can store them in dataframe form, inside the list we previously initialized:

```{R}
  summary_list[[sample_name]] <- data.frame(
    sample    = sample_name,
    plugin    = sd_plugin,
    chao_shen = sd_chao_shen,
    cwj       = sd_cwj,
    spanorm   = sd_spanorm,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
```

As the loop progresses, `summary_list` will get populated with a dataframe for each sample.

#### C. Memory clean up

These tables are pretty lightweight so it's not fundamental to have garbage collection, but it's still good practice to end the iteration with it:
```{R}
  rm(df_plugin, df_alt, df_spanorm)
  
  message("Done with ", sample_name)
}
```

This concludes our list.

### 3. Ranking and saving

At this point of the code, after all iterations have finished, we are left with a list of dataframes.
The point of the script is to rank the samples with the highest standard deviation, so before saving the results in a summary table, we should order the samples based on how big the sd is.

Since the metrics are different, it's likely that we will not get the same order across methods, so we calculate the ranking PER METHOD.

The first thing we need to do is to stitch the dataframes in the list together in one single dataframe.
Since there are 4 columns in each containing the values, we want to stack them vertically using `rind()`.

We implement a simple for loop to create our full dataframe:

```{R}
sd_df <- data.frame()

for (df in summary_list) {
  sd_df <- rbind(sd_df, df)
}
rownames(sd_df) <- NULL
```

There are better ways to do this (gemini suggested doing something with `do_call()` but that's mainly because of how R handles memory, which for 22 samples is just not a problem we should worry about).

We remove row names to avoid having two row 1s in the full dataframe.

We can now order the samples based on their standard deviations:

```{R}
ord_plugin    <- order(-sd_df$plugin,    sd_df$sample, na.last = TRUE)
ord_chao_shen <- order(-sd_df$chao_shen, sd_df$sample, na.last = TRUE)
ord_cwj       <- order(-sd_df$cwj,       sd_df$sample, na.last = TRUE)
ord_spanorm   <- order(-sd_df$spanorm,   sd_df$sample, na.last = TRUE)
```

In this way we have an ordered list of standard deviations per sample, that we can put in a new dataframe that we'll then write on file:

```{R}
ranked_table <- data.frame(
  "plugin"    = paste0(sd_df$sample[ord_plugin],    ": ", sd_df$plugin[ord_plugin]),
  "chao-shen" = paste0(sd_df$sample[ord_chao_shen], ": ", sd_df$chao_shen[ord_chao_shen]),
  "cwj"       = paste0(sd_df$sample[ord_cwj],       ": ", sd_df$cwj[ord_cwj]),
  "spanorm"   = paste0(sd_df$sample[ord_spanorm],   ": ", sd_df$spanorm[ord_spanorm]),
  check.names = FALSE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

We're done: we have a dataframe with a column for each method where we stored the ordered samples and their sd.

What's left is to just save it to an appropriate .csv:

```{R}
csv_file <- file.path(dir_tables, "entropy_sd_ranked.csv")
message("Saving ranked SD table to: ", csv_file)
write.csv(ranked_table, file = csv_file, row.names = FALSE)
```

We choose our .csv name inside our tables directory, and write the dataframe to it.
